newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater grand jury gets more time for probe.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater grand jury gets more time for probe.

text.p: A Whitewater grand jury was given an extra six months to investigate President Bill Clinton's business affairs on Tuesday after prosecutors said they had evidence justice may have been obstructed.

U.S. District Judge Susan Webber Wright granted a request by Whitewater special prosecutor Kenneth Starr to extend the life of the grand jury for six months. Its dismissal had been scheduled for May 7 but it will now work until Nov. 7.

"The United States submits, and the Court finds, that an extension of the grand jury is in the public interest ... in order for the grand jury to conclude its investigation of matters pending before it," Wright said in a ruling.
Starr filed a motion earlier on Tuesday saying the grand jury needed more time to pursue its probe.
"This grand jury has heard extensive evidence of possible obstruction of justice relating to matters within the Independent Counsel's jurisdiction," Starr wrote. He did not provide further details.
Starr is investigating whether the president or first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton played any part in fraudulent business deals in Arkansas in the mid-1980s, when Clinton was governor.

The probe was boosted recently when James McDougal, a former business partner of the Clintons in the failed Whitewater real estate venture, provided evidence to Starr's team in exchange for a lenient sentence for his own part in a string of fraudulent business deals.
McDougal was last week sentenced to three years in prison, a fraction of the maximum possible sentence facing him.

He said he reversed the testimony he gave at his trial last year and had corroborated allegations that Clinton pressured an Arkansas banker to extend an illegal $300,000 loan to McDougal's former wife Susan in 1986.
Clinton has sworn under oath that he played no part in winning the loan, but McDougal said the president lied.

Susan McDougal was sentenced to two years in prison for her part in the fraudulent loan, and is currently serving a contempt of court sentence for refusing to answer questions before the Whitewater grand jury in Little Rock, Arkansas.
Starr said in his motion filed on Tuesday that the information provided by James McDougal "emphasizes the continued need to obtain the testimony of Susan McDougal."
But Susan McDougal's attorney, Bobby McDaniel, said on Tuesday his client would not back down.

"Susan simply will not try to buy her freedom by participating in Mr. Starr's song and dance system of justice: sing his song and you dance out of jail," McDaniel told Reuters. "Susan remains steadfast in her refusal to cooperate with what she considers to be a tainted investigation."

Among the questions Susan McDougal refused to answer before the grand jury last September was whether Clinton had testified truthfully at the trial of her and her ex-husband. She has said she knows of nothing that would implicate the Clintons in any illegal activity.

Apart from Clinton's alleged involvement in winning the $300,000 loan -- part of which prosecutors say was funnelled into the struggling Whitewater venture -- Starr is also investigating whether Hillary Clinton helped James McDougal carry out a fraudulent land transaction on a real estate venture known as Castle Grande.
The first lady has acknowledged performing some legal work for the project, but denied any wrongdoing.
